unit.title: Operate in an autonomous team environment

summary: This unit teaches you to work in, and help lead, a self-managed team in a fabrication shop or on site: a team that plans, shares out, carries out and checks its own work within limits set by the business. You will learn to set clear targets, match people to tasks, make decisions together, help a team through its stages of development, keep safety and quality as shared duties, measure the team's performance, and solve problems so they stay solved.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). More and more fabrication work is done by small teams that are given a goal, such as a batch of gates by a set date, and then organise themselves to reach it. Nobody stands over each person telling them what to do next. That only works if every member takes responsibility, and if the team knows its limits.

At Level 3 you are expected to be one of the members who makes this work: helping to plan and share out tasks, speaking up about safety and quality, dealing with problems and disagreements fairly, and keeping the manager informed.
**Who it is for:** Level 3 welding trainees and fabricators who work in teams in a shop or on site, including those who act as team leader for a job or a week.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Know which decisions the team can make and which go to the manager, and stay inside the safety rules, budget and specification.
Help write clear, measurable targets that the whole team signs up to.
Break a job into tasks and match people to them by skill, qualification, safety and a fair share; build in training.
Take part in short daily meetings, choose the right way to make each decision, give and take feedback, and work with other teams.
Recognise the stages a team goes through, bring in new members, treat everyone with respect, and deal with conflict and slack work fairly.
Stop unsafe work, check each other's work, deal with rework honestly and keep the area in order.
Track output, quality and safety on a board everyone can see, and use the figures to improve, not to blame.
Use facts, a fishbone diagram, the 5 Whys and Plan–Do–Check–Act, then make the improvement the new standard.
Keep the manager and other teams informed, keep commitments, and learn from each job.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on autonomous teams, limits of authority, goals, roles, decisions, problem solving, improvement, performance, team development, safety, fairness and reporting.
A **written paper**: short answers that need exact terms (for example forming, root cause, kaizen, minutes, team charter, rework) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: producing a batch of brackets as a self-managed team, with ground rules, a skills matrix, a progress board and a review; and solving a real quality problem as a team, with a fishbone diagram, the 5 Whys, a trial and a short presentation.

blocks.note: In the practical tasks the assessor watches how you work with the others: whether you share the work fairly, check each other, speak up, listen and keep to the facts. A good finished batch is not enough on its own.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: An **autonomous** (self-managed) team is given a goal and the resources to reach it, and then plans, shares out, carries out and checks its own work, within limits agreed with management. The members agree the order of work, decide who does what, solve day-to-day problems and track their own output and quality.

head: Point
Closely supervised team
Self-managed team
rows: The team, inside the plan and budget it is given
The supervisor gives each person a task
The team, using its skills matrix
The team, and it calls the manager only for matters outside its limits
Members check each other; the inspector still inspects
The team, on a board everyone can see

ul: **Faster decisions:** problems on the shop floor are settled where they happen, without waiting for a supervisor.
**Wider skills:** members rotate tasks, so the team can cover absences and peaks.
**Commitment:** people work harder for targets they helped to set.
**Better ideas:** the people doing the work see the improvements first.

blocks.p: Self-managed does not mean "no rules". The team works inside the business's safety rules, the law, the budget, the client's specification and the delivery dates. The limits should be agreed with the manager when the team is set up and written down, usually in a **team charter**: the team's purpose, goals, members and roles, limits of authority and ground rules.

head: The team usually decides
The manager usually decides
rows: The order of the day's tasks
Who does each task, and how to cover an absence
Small changes to methods, jigs and layout
Housekeeping and its own ground rules
Prices, delivery dates and anything promised to a client
Changes to the design, materials or specification
Spending outside the budget, such as a new machine
Accepting work that does not meet the specification

blocks.note: Safety rules are never inside the team's power to relax, not even by a unanimous vote. If the team is not sure whether a decision is its own, it asks before acting, and it tells the manager what it has decided.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Many Jamaican fabrication shops are small, and the owner is often the manager, estimator and salesman at once. A team that organises its own work, reports honestly and only brings the owner the decisions that are truly the owner's frees him to win the next job.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Goals, roles and sharing the work

blocks.p: A target the team can use is **SMART**: Specific, Measurable, Agreed (or Achievable), Realistic and Time-bound.

head: Weak target
Why it fails
Better target
rows: "Work hard on the railings this week."
Nothing to measure; no finish time
"Fit and weld 10 railing panels by Thursday at 4 p.m., all passing inspection."
"No more than 2 welds rejected per 50 inspected by the end of the month."
"30 frames a week, square within ±2 mm, for the next four weeks."

blocks.p: The whole team should help set its targets. People are more committed to a target they helped to set, and the members often know better than anyone what is realistic. A target set too high is ignored; one set too low wastes the team's ability.

flow: Read the job card and drawings together
List the tasks: check materials, mark out, cut, fit and tack, weld, clean, paint, load, fit on site
Estimate the time for each and note which must be done in order
Match people to tasks using the skills matrix
Set daily targets and put the plan on a board
Check progress each day and move people where a task falls behind

blocks.p: A **skills matrix** is a simple chart of who can do each task, at what level, and who needs training. It is how the team shares out work fairly and safely, and how it plans training.

ul: Give coded or certified welding only to members qualified for it, and hazardous tasks only to members trained for them. Nobody works alone on a hazardous task.
Share the heavy, hot and boring jobs fairly. If one member always gets the easy jobs, resentment builds quickly. Agree an open way of sharing and review it each week.
Build training into the plan: a learner works alongside a member who can train others, when the job allows the time.

blocks.p: **Multi-skilling** means training each member to do several jobs. Rotating tasks (cutting one day, fitting the next) is a little slower at first, but it means that if one person is absent, others can cover, and that nobody is stuck on one tiring task all week. If only one member can do a vital task, the whole job stops when that person is off sick: train a second member before that happens.

blocks.h: Sharing the load during the day

ul: When one member is overloaded and another is waiting (for material, for paint to dry), move the free member to help, if he or she can do that task safely.
When a member finishes early, he or she checks the board or asks the team what to take next, rather than waiting to be told or starting something nobody agreed.
When someone is absent, the team reviews the plan first and shares out the work safely; it does not simply carry on one short or drop the checks.

blocks.p: **Ground rules** are the team's own written agreements about how it works: start and finish times, breaks, phone use, how meetings run, how decisions are made, how tools are signed out, how disagreements are raised. Writing them down means everyone knows what is expected, and new members can read them on day one.

A short meeting (often 10 minutes or less), held standing at the work area at the start of the shift, keeps everyone on today's work. Standing keeps it short; holding it at the board means the facts are in front of everyone.

ul: What did we finish yesterday against the target?
What is today's target, and who is doing what?
Any safety points, absences, shortages or problems?
Anything that needs the manager or another team?

blocks.p: Longer weekly meetings need an agenda, a time limit and **minutes**: a short written record of the decisions and the actions agreed, each with a person and a date. Read the actions at the start of the next meeting.

head: Method
How it works
Use it when
rows: The team leader for the job decides, after hearing views if there is time
Time is short, or the matter is small and someone must simply choose
The nearest trained person acts at once, as the plan says
Fire, injury, a gas or electrical emergency: there is no time to discuss
The choice with the most votes is taken
A quick choice between options that are all safe and acceptable, where some members may not agree
Everyone discusses until all can support the decision, even if it was not their first choice
There is time, and the whole team must back the choice to make it work
Try the options on a small scale, measure, then choose
Members disagree about which method is better, and the facts can settle it
Pass it to the manager with the facts and the options
The matter is outside the team's limits

blocks.note: Some things are never decided by a vote: safety rules, the law and the client's specification. A team that "votes" to skip a fire watch has made no decision at all, and any member should refuse to go along with it.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Talk about the **work**, not the person: "The diagonals on this frame differ by 6 mm" rather than "You are careless".
Be specific, be prompt, and give the reason it matters.
Give praise in front of the team and criticism in private.
When you receive feedback, listen to the end, ask questions to understand, and thank the person, even if you disagree. Then check the facts.
Shared equipment (a crane, forklift, plasma table or scissor lift) is planned between the team leaders: agree times, not first-come-first-served.
Never use or interfere with equipment another team has locked off, and never remove another person's lock or tag.
When your work affects another team's (fixing positions, access, noise, sparks), agree it with them before you start, and get approval if it changes the design.

blocks.h: Reporting to management and keeping commitments

ul: A self-managed team still reports its progress, so that the business can plan, order materials and give clients true dates.
Report **early**: as soon as the team knows a target or date is at risk, tell the manager, with the facts, the new estimate and the options. Bad news gets worse with age.

Matters that touch the client (a late delivery, a fault in work already sent out, a drawing error) go to the manager, who agrees a fix with the client. Never hide a mistake, and never quietly make a change to the design.
If the team finds a drawing error part-way through, it stops that part, tells the designer through the manager, and waits for the agreed change.

blocks.p: Most new teams go through the same stages (from a model by Bruce Tuckman). Knowing them helps you understand what is happening and what will help.

head: Stage
What you see
How a Level 3 member helps
rows: Members are new, polite and unsure of their roles; they look to the leader
Make the goal, the ground rules and each person's role clear
Disagreements about methods, roles and who does what; some loud arguments
Keep the talk on facts, listen to each side, agree fair ways of working and of settling disputes
The team settles on its ways of working; rules are followed and trust grows, but members still check before acting
Write down the agreed methods and ground rules; encourage skill sharing
The team works well with little supervision, solves its own problems and meets its targets
Recognise good work, bring in improvements, help new members fit in
The job ends and the team breaks up or moves on
Review the job, record the lessons, thank people

blocks.p: A change of members, a new leader or a big change in the work can send a team back a stage. That is normal; help it through again.

ol: Safety induction first: the site rules, exits, fire extinguishers, first aid, the machines and their hazards.
Introduce each member and say who to ask about what.
Explain the goal, the plan, the targets and the ground rules.
Pair the new member with an experienced **buddy** (mentor) for the first days or weeks.
Check his or her skills against the skills matrix (for example with a test piece) before giving a task that suits them.
Include the new member in the daily meeting from the first day.
After a week or so, review how they are settling in and what training they need, and update the skills matrix.

ul: Every member is treated with the same respect, whatever their sex, age, religion, parish, accent, background or experience.

"Jokes" that pick on someone's accent, home district, religion, sex or appearance are not harmless. Say plainly that it is not acceptable, support the person targeted, and report it if it continues. Harassment and discrimination break company policy and, in many cases, the law.
Information, tasks and training are shared equally. A leader who gives instructions only to some members, or ignores questions from others, damages the team and must be told.
Disagree with ideas, never attack the person.

flow: Deal with it early, before it grows
Talk in private, calmly, with the people involved
Let each side explain, and listen without interrupting
Separate the facts from the feelings, and find what both sides need
Agree a solution, or a fair way to decide (for example a trial)
Check later that it has worked; go to the manager if it has not

blocks.p: **Accountability** means each member answers for his or her own work and its results. The welder is responsible first for the quality of each weld; the team as a whole is responsible for the job. When a member's work or time-keeping slips:

ul: Do not gossip, freeze the person out, complain behind their back or leave their work undone "to make a point".
One member (often the leader or someone the person trusts) talks to them **privately and soon**, about facts: "You arrived after 8:00 on five days" or "Four of your last 15 welds failed".
Listen: there may be a reason, such as illness, a family problem, a machine fault or a task they were never shown.
Agree what will change, what help the team can give (coaching, a change of task) and when you will review it. Note the agreement.
If there is no improvement, or the problem is serious (safety, honesty), it goes to the manager: discipline is outside the team's authority.

blocks.p: Thank people for specific good work, in front of the team: "Sasha's jig cut our fit-up time in half." It costs nothing, shows what good looks like and keeps people trying. Favouritism, such as always giving one person the easy jobs, does the opposite.
In a self-managed team there may be no supervisor watching every task, so each member looks after his or her own safety and that of the others.

ul: **Any member who sees danger may stop the job**, without blame, whatever their rank or experience. Safety comes before targets.
Before a job, the team looks at the hazards together (hot work, lifting, grinding, working at height, electricity) and agrees the controls: screens, fire watch, PPE, safe lifting, safe access.
Members check each other's set-up and PPE and speak up politely when something is wrong.
Safety tasks are shared on a rota: checking extinguishers, the first-aid box, leads and ladders.
Near misses and hazards are reported and discussed at the daily meeting, so the cause is fixed before someone is hurt.
Nobody may skip a safety step to finish early: no missing fire watch, no unguarded machine, no working at height without safe access.

blocks.note: A trainee may feel it is not his or her place to stop a job. Make it clear in the ground rules that it is, and back up anyone who does so in good faith, even if it turns out there was no danger.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Each person checks his or her own work, and members check each other's at key points: for example a frame's sizes and diagonals before it is fully welded.
A **first-off check**: the first item of a batch is checked against the drawing before the rest are made. One error found then saves twenty later.
A second pair of eyes catches mistakes before they cost more. The purpose is to find errors, not to name the person who made them.
**Rework** (work done again because it failed) costs time, material and goodwill. Track it, and find its cause.
If faulty work has already gone out, tell the manager at once so a fix can be agreed with the client. Hoping the client will not notice, or swapping parts quietly, destroys trust.

blocks.p: A tidy work area is a shared duty because everyone uses it, and clutter causes trips, lost tools, fires and delays. Many shops use **5S**:

head: S
Meaning
In a welding bay
rows: Scrap, broken tools and old drawings go
Shadow board for hand tools; marked racks for offcuts
Sweep, clear spatter and slag, check leads as you go
Agree how the area is kept, and write it down
A checklist for the end of each shift
Keep it up as a habit, and check it
A weekly check by a different member each week

ul: Running out of consumables stops work. Track how many are used each week and set a **re-order level**: the stock at which you re-order.
Re-order level = usage per week × weeks the supplier takes to deliver + a small safety stock. Example: 5 packs of discs a week, 2-week delivery, safety stock of 3: re-order when stock falls to 13.
Look after tools and equipment as if they were your own, and report damage at once.

blocks.p: A team that manages itself must know whether it is on track. A few simple measures, shown where everyone can see them, tell it that.

head: Measure (key performance indicator)
Example
Collected from
rows: Frames finished each day against a target of 24
The board, marked at the end of each shift
Welds or items rejected at inspection each week; rework hours
Near misses reported; injuries; safety checks done
The near-miss book and the rota
Hours used against hours planned for the job

ul: Choose a few measures the team can control and that matter to the business. Too many measures means none is watched.
Percentage of target = actual ÷ target × 100. A day of 21 frames against 24 is 87.5%.

**Leading** measures (near misses reported, safety checks done, first-off checks made) warn you before something goes wrong. **Lagging** measures (injuries, rejects, late jobs) tell you after. A month with no injuries does not prove the shop is safe; near-miss reports show where the next injury could come from.

blocks.p: A board on the workshop wall, showing each day's target and actual output, quality and safety figures, lets everyone see at once whether the team is on track. It turns the daily meeting into a look at facts, not opinions.

ul: Look at **trends** over several days or weeks, not one bad day.
When a figure drops, look for the causes (absence, a breakdown, late material, rework, a new task) before deciding what to do. Do not simply work longer hours or cut the target.
Never use the measures to blame or shame one person. If people fear the board, they stop reporting honestly, and then the figures are useless.
Use the figures to spot problems early, find their causes and try improvements.

sections.title: Solving problems and improving the work

blocks.p: A problem that is not clearly stated cannot be solved. Write it in one sentence, with measured facts: what, where, how many, since when. "Paint is flaking on 9 of the last 30 gates, within two months of fitting" is a problem statement. "The painters are useless" is an opinion that blames people and points nowhere.

ul: Collect data: when it happens, where, on which machine or batch, who was working, what material.
Look at the work itself, not only at what people remember.
Keep the talk on the process, not on who is to blame.

blocks.p: A **fishbone diagram** (also called an Ishikawa diagram) puts the problem at the "head" and sorts the possible causes along "bones" under headings. Common headings, the **6 Ms**:

head: Heading
Example causes for warped frames
rows: No agreed welding sequence; no tacking pattern
Bench not flat; no clamps or jig
Bent stock; different wall thickness from a new supplier
New member not shown the sequence; rushed at the end of the day
Diagonals not checked before full welding; tape damaged
Frames left in the sun on one side; rain on hot welds

blocks.p: Ask "why?" about the problem, then about the answer, and so on, usually about five times, until you reach a cause that, once fixed, stops the problem coming back: the **root cause**. Fixing only the first answer (the symptom) means the problem returns.

flow: Frames are out of square. Why?
They pull over when the long welds are done. Why?
All the welds on one side are done first. Why?
Each welder uses his own order. Why?
No welding sequence has ever been agreed or written down: the root cause

head: Stage
What the team does
rows: Choose a change that tackles the root cause, decide how to measure success, and agree who does what
Try the change on a small scale, such as a few items
Measure the results the same way as before the change, and compare
If it worked, make it the standard method: write it down and train everyone. If not, learn why and go round again

ul: Make the comparison **fair**: measure the trial items with the same test, the same tools and the same method as the old ones.
Change one thing at a time. If you change the paint and the timing together, you will not know which helped.
Keep measuring after the change becomes standard, to be sure it lasts.

blocks.p: **Kaizen** is a Japanese word for continuous improvement in small steps, by everyone, every day. Good ideas often come from the newest or quietest member. Listen to each suggestion, thank the person, test it safely on a small scale and, if it works, make it standard. Never try an untested idea on a customer's job.

ul: Hold the review soon after the job, while people remember, with everyone who took part, for about half an hour.
Gather the facts first: hours planned and used, material, inspection results, rework, near misses, the client's comments.
Ask three questions: **What went well? What did not? What will we change next time?**
Keep to the work and the methods, not blame, and make sure the quieter members are heard.
For each lesson, agree an **action, a person and a date**, and keep the notes with the job file. At the start of the next similar job, read them and check the actions were done.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and talk it through with your instructor.

ul: I can explain what a self-managed team is and how it differs from a closely supervised one.
I can give examples of decisions the team makes and decisions that go to the manager.
I can explain what a team charter and ground rules are for.
I can help write a SMART target.
I can break a job into tasks and use a skills matrix to share them fairly and safely.
I can explain why multi-skilling and rotation protect the team.
I can take part in a short daily meeting and record actions in minutes.
I can choose a suitable way to make a decision, and say which matters are never voted on.
I can give and take feedback about the work, not the person.
I can work with other teams over shared equipment and changes.
I can report problems and risks to the manager early.
I can name and describe the stages of team development, and help a team through them.
I can bring a new member into the team safely.
I can challenge disrespect and unfairness, and help settle a conflict.
I can deal with a member whose work is slipping, fairly and privately.
I can stop unsafe work and help the team keep safety a shared duty.
I can carry out first-off and peer checks, and deal with rework honestly.
I can explain 5S and set a re-order level.
I can track performance on a board and use the figures to improve, not to blame.
I can use a fishbone diagram, the 5 Whys and PDCA to solve a problem, and hold an end-of-job review.

terms: 5S
Sort, set in order, shine, standardise, sustain: a method for keeping a work area in order
Accountability
A member's duty to answer for his or her own work and its results
Autonomous (self-managed) team
A team that plans, shares out, does and checks its own work within agreed limits
Buddy (mentor)
An experienced member paired with a new one to guide him or her
Consensus
A decision that every member can support, reached by discussion
Fishbone diagram
A cause-and-effect chart that sorts possible causes under headings; also called an Ishikawa diagram
First-off check
Checking the first item of a batch against the drawing before making the rest
Forming, storming, norming, performing
The usual stages a new team goes through
Ground rules
The team's written agreements on how it works
Kaizen
Continuous improvement in small steps by everyone
Key performance indicator (KPI)
A measure used to track how well the team is doing
Limits of authority
The boundary between the team's decisions and the manager's
Majority vote
A decision that takes the choice with the most votes
Minutes
The written record of a meeting's decisions and actions
Multi-skilling
Training each member to do several different tasks
Near miss
An event that could have caused injury or damage but did not
PDCA
Plan, Do, Check, Act: a cycle for testing and making improvements
Re-order level
The stock level at which more is ordered
Rework
Work done again because it failed inspection
Root cause
The underlying cause which, once fixed, stops a problem coming back
Skills matrix
A chart of who can do each task and who needs training
SMART
Specific, measurable, agreed, realistic and time-bound: the marks of a useful target
Target
A level of output or result agreed in advance
Team charter
The document setting out a team's purpose, goals, roles, limits and ground rules

c1.title: Security doors for a housing scheme in Old Harbour
c1.text: A self-managed team of five at a shop in Old Harbour, St Catherine, is making 30 steel security doors for a housing scheme in four weeks. Its charter says the team decides the order of work and who does what, and may spend up to J$20 000 a month on small tools; changes to materials, prices or dates go to the manager. Keisha is the only member qualified to weld the hinge brackets to the code the client requires. The team's first draft target reads: "Do 15 doors properly next week." In week three, the galvaniser says the first batch will come back four days late.

c2.title: A trainee team building a shed in Kingston
c2.text: Six Level 3 trainees at a training centre in Kingston form a self-managed team to build a steel shed over a term. In week two, Ricardo and Dane argue loudly about how to make the roof trusses. Jason, leader for that week, gives instructions only to the men and ignores Nicole's questions. In week three, Jermaine transfers in from another centre. By week six the team keeps to its written ground rules and trust is growing, but members still check with the instructor before changing the plan.

c3.title: Flaking paint on balcony rails in Negril
c3.text: A team at a shop in Negril, Westmoreland, made 40 painted steel balcony rails for a guest house near the sea. Three months after fitting, the paint is flaking on 14 of them. The team's records show the rails were blast-cleaned in the afternoon and primed the next morning, because another team uses the compressor every morning and no schedule for sharing it has ever been agreed.

c4.title: The team board at a shop in Lucea
c4.text: A self-managed team at a fabrication shop in Lucea, Hanover, makes steel window frames. Its board shows a target of 24 frames a day and actual output of 22 on Monday, 24 on Tuesday, 18 on Wednesday and 23 on Thursday. Two near misses were reported this month and there were no injuries. Five of Courtney's last 20 welds were rejected at inspection.

c5.title: Fitting grilles at a health centre in Black River
c5.text: A team is fitting steel security grilles and a ramp handrail at a health centre in Black River, St Elizabeth, while an electricians' team works in the same building. The electricians ask the welders to leave out two grille fixings so that their conduit can pass. On the second day the ground under a ladder at the side of the building is soft after rain; Shanelle, a trainee, feels the ladder shift but is unsure whether it is her place to say so. The team holds a review when the job is finished.

questions.q: Under its charter, which of these can the door team decide without the manager?
o: Fitting a cheaper hinge than the one specified
Moving the delivery date back by a week
Paying double time instead of time and a half
Buying J$15 000 of new clamps this month
questions.why: Spending within the agreed allowance is the team's decision. Changes to materials, dates and pay affect the client or the business, so they go to the manager.

questions.q: What is the best long-term answer to Keisha being the only member qualified for the hinge brackets?
o: Use the skills matrix to train and qualify a second member
Keep Keisha on hinge brackets only, so they never fall behind
Let others weld them when she is off, and have her check later
Ask the client to accept any welder on days she is absent
questions.why: If the only qualified person is absent, that part of the job stops. Training and qualifying another member removes the risk; unqualified welding of coded joints is never acceptable.

questions.q: Which rewrite of the draft target would the team find most useful?
o: "Fifteen doors done properly, working as hard as we can"
"As many doors as we can, all of them done properly"
"Fifteen doors passed at inspection by Friday at noon"
"Fifteen doors next week, with everyone doing his best"
questions.why: A useful target is specific, measurable and time-bound. "Passed at inspection" makes "properly" measurable, and "Friday at noon" sets the deadline; effort and good intentions cannot be measured.

questions.q: What should the team do when it hears the galvanising will be four days late?
o: Wait to see whether the galvaniser catches up before saying anything
Phone the client and agree a new delivery date themselves
Tell the manager now, with the new dates and the options
Paint the doors instead of galvanising them to keep the date
questions.why: Delivery dates and finishes are outside the team's limits, and early warning lets the business plan and tell the client in time. Changing the specified finish to save time is not the team's decision.

questions.q: How should a Level 3 member handle the shouting match over the trusses?
o: Calm it down, hear each one's reasons and agree how to decide
Let the louder of the two decide, so the work can carry on
Tell them both to stop and leave all decisions to the instructor
Call an immediate vote before either of them has explained
questions.why: This is the storming stage. Keeping the talk on facts, listening to both sides and agreeing a fair way to decide settles the dispute and builds the team. Volume or a rushed vote settles nothing.

questions.q: What should be done about Jason ignoring Nicole's questions?
o: Leave it, as the leader for the week may run things his own way
Tell Nicole to pass her questions through one of the men
Complain about Jason in the group chat so that he gets the message
Speak to Jason privately and see that Nicole is told the same
questions.why: Every member is owed the same information and respect. Speaking to Jason privately is fair and quick; if it continues, it is reported. Public complaints or work-arounds leave the unfairness in place.

questions.q: What should happen before Jermaine starts work on his first morning?
o: Nothing, since he is already a Level 3 trainee
Two weeks of watching before he does any task
A safety induction and a check of his skills
Reading the job file alone to find his own way
questions.why: A new member must know the site's hazards, exits and rules before working, and his skills are checked against the skills matrix before he is given a task that suits him, with a buddy to guide him.

questions.q: Which stage of development has the team reached by week six?
o: Forming
Storming
Norming
Performing
questions.why: Agreed rules that are kept and growing trust mark the norming stage. A performing team also works with little supervision and solves its own problems, which this team is not yet doing.

questions.q: Which is the best problem statement for the team to start from?
o: The painters did a poor job on the guest house balcony rails
Paint flaking on 14 of 40 rails, three months after fitting
Our paint is no good and must be changed for another at once
The guest house owner keeps on complaining to us about them
questions.why: A problem statement gives measured facts (what, how many, since when) without blaming anyone or jumping to a solution. The other statements are opinions that point the team in the wrong direction.

questions.q: On the fishbone diagram, under which heading do "salt air and morning dew on the steel" belong?
o: Materials
Methods
Environment
Measurement
questions.why: Conditions round the work, such as humidity, salt air, rain and heat, go under environment (sometimes called mother nature). Sorting causes under headings makes sure no group of causes is missed.

questions.q: The team's 5 Whys run: flaking, poor adhesion, rust under the primer, steel left overnight after blasting, compressor not free in the mornings. Which root cause should the team fix?
o: The primer did not stick properly to the steel
No agreed schedule for sharing the compressor
Rust formed on the blasted steel overnight
The rails were primed on the following morning
questions.why: The root cause is the one at the bottom of the chain which, once fixed, stops the rest happening. Without a compressor schedule, blasting will keep drifting into the afternoon and the rust will come back.

questions.q: The team trials blasting and priming on the same morning. How should it judge whether the change worked?
o: Look only at the new rails, as they are what changed
Test the new and old rails in the same way
Ask the guest house owner whether they look better
Change to a new brand of paint for the trial as well
questions.why: In the Check stage the comparison must be fair: the same test, the same tools, the same method. Changing two things at once would leave the team unable to tell which one helped.

questions.q: For the four days so far, what percentage of the target has the team reached?
o: About 87%
About 96%
About 110%
About 91%
questions.why: Actual 22 + 24 + 18 + 23 = 87 frames; target 4 × 24 = 96. 87 ÷ 96 × 100 = 90.6%. Wednesday's dip is the day to look into for causes.

questions.q: Why is it useful to count near misses in a month with no injuries?
o: They show which members are careless
They show hazards before anyone is hurt
They prove the shop is already safe
They matter only once an injury happens
questions.why: Near misses are a leading measure: each one shows where the next injury could come from. Using them to blame people stops people reporting them.

questions.q: After Wednesday's 18, a member suggests cutting the daily target to 20 for good. What is the best response?
o: Find what caused Wednesday's dip before changing the target
Agree, so that the team can meet its target every single day
Keep the target and make up Wednesday's frames with overtime
Find out which member had a bad day and have a word with him
questions.why: One low day is not a trend, and the other three days were close to 24, so the target looks realistic. Look for the cause first (absence, a breakdown, late material, rework); cutting the target, working longer or blaming someone does not fix it.

questions.q: How should the team deal with Courtney's rejected welds?
o: Put his reject count up on the team board beside his name
Talk with him privately about the facts and agree some help
Take him off welding for good and give him only grinding work
Report him to the manager for discipline straight away
questions.why: Five rejects in 20 is a fact to discuss privately: there may be a cause such as a machine fault or a technique he was never shown. Agree help and a review date; shaming him on the board would stop honest reporting.

questions.q: What should the team do about the electricians' request to leave out two fixings?
o: Leave the fixings out, since the electricians asked first
Refuse, as the grilles are not the electricians' business
Fit the fixings anyway and let the electricians work round them
Agree a solution with them and get it approved first
questions.why: Work that affects another team is agreed with that team, and anything that changes the design, such as fewer fixings on a security grille, needs approval before it is done.

questions.q: What should happen about the ladder on soft ground?
o: Shanelle speaks up and the ladder is moved to a firm base
She keeps quiet and leaves all safety calls to the team leader
She carries on carefully, as the job is nearly done
She waits and raises it later, at the end-of-job review
questions.why: Any member who sees danger may stop the job, trainees included, and the team should back her. A ladder that shifts on soft ground can throw the user off; it needs a firm, level base or other access.

questions.q: Which record from the review is most likely to change how the next job goes?
o: A note of who caused each problem
A general promise to do better next time
The hours each person worked on site
Actions, each with a person and a date
questions.why: Lessons only change things when someone is named to act by a set date, and the actions are checked at the start of the next job. Blame and vague promises change nothing.

questions.q: A team sorted, tidied and cleaned its welding bay in a 5S drive. A month later it is cluttered again. Which S has the team failed to keep up?
o: Sustain
Sort
Shine
Set in order
questions.why: Sustain means making the routine a habit and checking it, for example with a weekly check by a different member. Without it, the first three S's slowly come undone.
